note: imperfect: نتمنّى nitmannā (I hope), يتمنّى yitmannā (he hopes). Everyday 'hopefully' is إن شاء الله / يا ريت.

ex_en: I expect he'll come late
note: imperfect: نتوقّع nitwagga3 (I expect), يتوقّع yitwagga3 (he expects)

ex_en: I don't believe you, you're joking!
note: imperfect: نصدّق nSaddig (I believe), يصدّق ySaddig (he believes). ق = g.

ex_en: I doubt he told the truth
note: imperfect: نشك nshukk (I doubt), يشك yshukk (he doubts)

ex_en: I decided to quit smoking
note: imperfect: نقرّر ngarrir (I decide), يقرّر ygarrir (he decides). ق = g.

ex_en: Choose whichever you like
note: imperfect: نختار nikhtār (I choose), يختار yikhtār (he chooses)

ex_en: I prefer coffee to tea
note: imperfect: نفضّل nfaDDil (I prefer), يفضّل yfaDDil (he prefers)

ex_en: I'm learning Italian
note: imperfect: نتعلّم nit3allam (I learn), يتعلّم yit3allam (he learns). الطليان iT-Tilyān = Italian (language), lit. the Italians.

ex_en: He memorized the Quran when he was young
note: imperfect: نحفظ ni7faDH (I memorize), يحفظ yi7faDH (he memorizes). القرآن keeps q.

ex_en: You'll regret it if you don't come
note: imperfect: نندم nindam (I regret), يندم yindam (he regrets)

en: to get upset; to be offended
ex_en: Don't be upset with me
note: imperfect: نزعل niz3al (I get upset), يزعل yiz3al (he gets upset)

en: to get annoyed; to get fed up
ex_en: I got fed up with the traffic
note: imperfect: نتقلّق nitgallag (I get annoyed), يتقلّق yitgallag (he gets annoyed). Libyan; مقلّق mgallag = annoyed, bored. ق = g.

ex_en: He got angry with me and didn't speak to me
note: imperfect: نتغشّش nitghashshash (I get angry), يتغشّش yitghashshash (he gets angry). Libyan/Maghrebi; مغشّش mghashshash = angry.

ex_en: You scared me! I didn't hear you coming
note: imperfect: نخلع nikhla3 (I get scared), يخلع yikhla3 (he gets scared). Maghrebi; خلعة khal3a = fright.

ex_en: I was so happy when I saw you
note: imperfect: نفرح nifra7 (I am happy), يفرح yifra7 (he is happy)

en: to be surprised; to find strange
ex_en: I was surprised he didn't come
note: imperfect: نستغرب nistaghrib (I am surprised), يستغرب yistaghrib (he is surprised)

ex_en: I dreamt about you last night
note: imperfect: نحلم ni7lam (I dream), يحلم yi7lam (he dreams)

ex_en: He doesn't take care of his health
note: imperfect: نهتم nihtamm (I care), يهتم yihtamm (he cares)

ex_en: I missed you so much, brother
note: imperfect: نتوحّش nitwa77ash (I miss), يتوحّش yitwa77ash (he misses). Maghrebi; وحشتني wa7ashtni also heard.

ex_en: I miss my mother's cooking
note: imperfect: نشتاق nishtāg (I long for), يشتاق yishtāg (he longs for). ق = g.

ex_en: He's very protective (jealous) of his sister
note: imperfect: نغير nghīr (I am jealous), يغير yghīr (he is jealous)

en: to be at a loss; to be confused
ex_en: I couldn't decide what to buy
note: imperfect: نحتار ni7tār (I am at a loss), يحتار yi7tār (he is at a loss)

ex_en: What do you intend to do after university?
note: imperfect: ننوي ninwi (I intend), ينوي yinwi (he intends). Participle ناوي nāwi 'intending' is very common.

ex_en: Focus with me for a moment
note: imperfect: نركّز nrakkiz (I concentrate), يركّز yrakkiz (he concentrates)

ex_en: I noticed he has changed
note: imperfect: نلاحظ nlā7iDH (I notice), يلاحظ ylā7iDH (he notices)

ex_en: He deserves all the best
note: imperfect: نستاهل nistāhil (I deserve), يستاهل yistāhil (he deserves)

ex_en: Be patient, everything will be fixed
note: imperfect: نصبر nuSbur (I am patient), يصبر yuSbur (he is patient)

en: to be shy; to be embarrassed
ex_en: Don't be shy, eat!
note: imperfect: نحشم ni7sham (I am shy), يحشم yi7sham (he is shy). Maghrebi; حشمة 7ashma = modesty, shame.

ex_en: I got used to the new job
note: imperfect: نتعوّد nit3awwad (I get used to), يتعوّد yit3awwad (he gets used to)

ex_en: You must respect your elders
note: imperfect: نحترم ni7tarim (I respect), يحترم yi7tarim (he respects)

ex_en: Forgive me, I didn't mean it
note: imperfect: نسامح nsāmi7 (I forgive), يسامح ysāmi7 (he forgives)

en: to get bored; to get tired of
ex_en: I'm bored of sitting at home
note: imperfect: نمل nmill (I get bored), يمل ymill (he gets bored)

ex_en: I think it's going to rain today
note: imperfect: نضن nDunn (I think), يضن yDunn (he thinks). ظ is pronounced like ض in Libyan; spelling ظن also used.

ex_en: Work out how much we owe you
note: imperfect: نحسب ni7sib (I count), يحسب yi7sib (he counts)

ex_en: Where do you work? I work at a company
note: imperfect: نخدم nikhdim (I work), يخدم yikhdim (he works). Also 'to function': الكرهبة ما تخدمش 'the car doesn't work'.

ex_en: I bought new clothes at the market
note: imperfect: نشري nishri (I buy), يشري yishri (he buys)

ex_en: He sold the old car
note: imperfect: نبيع nbī3 (I sell), يبيع ybī3 (he sells)

ex_en: How much did you pay for it?
note: imperfect: ندفع nidfa3 (I pay), يدفع yidfa3 (he pays)

ex_en: Pay the bill, I'll pay you back soon
note: imperfect: نخلّص nkhalliS (I pay), يخلّص ykhalliS (he pays). Very common Libyan/Maghrebi 'pay'. خلاص khlāS = payment, salary.

ex_en: Open the door, someone's knocking
note: imperfect: نحل n7ill (I open), يحل y7ill (he opens). Typical Libyan 'open' (also 'to solve'). محلول ma7lūl = open.

ex_en: The shop opens at eight
note: imperfect: نفتح nifta7 (I open), يفتح yifta7 (he opens). حل 7all is the more colloquial 'open'.

ex_en: Close the window, it's windy
note: imperfect: نسكّر nsakkir (I close), يسكّر ysakkir (he closes)

ex_en: I have to fix the car
note: imperfect: نصلّح nSalli7 (I fix), يصلّح ySalli7 (he fixes)

ex_en: I fixed your phone, it works now
note: imperfect: نسڨّم nsaggim (I fix), يسڨّم ysaggim (he fixes). Libyan/Tunisian; also spelled سقّم or سگّم. Also 'to arrange, set straight'.

ex_en: He's building a new house
note: imperfect: نبني nibni (I build), يبني yibni (he builds)

ex_en: Lend me two hundred dinars
note: imperfect: نسلّف nsallif (I lend), يسلّف ysallif (he lends)

ex_en: I borrowed money from my brother
note: imperfect: نتسلّف nitsallaf (I borrow), يتسلّف yitsallaf (he borrows)

ex_en: We rented a flat near the sea
note: imperfect: نكري nikri (I rent), يكري yikri (he rents). Means both 'rent (from)' and 'rent out'.

ex_en: I'm saving up to get married
note: imperfect: نوفّر nwaffir (I save), يوفّر ywaffir (he saves)

ex_en: I spent the whole salary
note: imperfect: نصرف nuSruf (I spend), يصرف yuSruf (he spends). شهرية shahriyya = monthly salary.

ex_en: Al-Ittihad won the match
note: imperfect: نربح nurba7 (I win), يربح yurba7 (he wins). Al-Ittihad = Tripoli football club.

ex_ar: خسرنا فلوس هلبة في التجارة هذي
ex_en: We lost a lot of money in this business
note: imperfect: نخسر nikhsar (I lose), يخسر yikhsar (he loses). Also 'to spoil (food)': خاسر khāsir = spoiled, broken.

ex_en: Don't waste your time
note: imperfect: نضيّع nDayyi3 (I lose), يضيّع yDayyi3 (he loses)

ex_en: I'm studying for the exam
note: imperfect: ندرس nidris (I study), يدرس yidris (he studies). قرا grā is the everyday word for studying at school.

ex_en: I passed the exam, thank God
note: imperfect: ننجح ninja7 (I pass), ينجح yinja7 (he passes)

ex_en: He failed maths
note: imperfect: نسقط nusguT (I fail), يسقط yusguT (he fails). ق = g.

ex_en: He teaches at a primary school
note: imperfect: نقرّي ngarri (I teach), يقرّي ygarri (he teaches). Causative of قرا grā; ق = g.

ex_en: Do you want me to help you?
note: imperfect: نعاون n3āwin (I help), يعاون y3āwin (he helps). Everyday Libyan 'help'.

ex_en: Help me carry the box
note: imperfect: نساعد nsā3id (I help), يساعد ysā3id (he helps)

ex_en: I use my phone for everything
note: imperfect: نستعمل nista3mil (I use), يستعمل yista3mil (he uses)

ex_en: Try on the shirt before you buy it
note: imperfect: نجرّب njarrib (I try), يجرّب yjarrib (he tries)

ex_en: I'll try to come early
note: imperfect: نحاول n7āwil (I try), يحاول y7āwil (he tries)

ex_en: He broke the glass while washing up
note: imperfect: نكسر niksir (I break), يكسر yiksir (he breaks). Intransitive تكسّر tkassar 'got broken'.

ex_en: He broke my phone
note: imperfect: نخرّب nkharrib (I ruin), يخرّب ykharrib (he ruins)

ex_en: He loves drawing in his notebook
note: imperfect: نرسم nirsim (I draw), يرسم yirsim (he draws)

ex_en: Print this paper for me
note: imperfect: نطبع niTba3 (I print), يطبع yiTba3 (he prints)

ex_en: Sign here please
note: imperfect: نمضي nimDi (I sign), يمضي yimDi (he signs). Maghrebi; مضاء mDā = signature.

ex_en: I booked a ticket to Istanbul
note: imperfect: نحجز ni7jiz (I book), يحجز yi7jiz (he books)

ex_en: I got my salary today
note: imperfect: نستلم nistlim (I receive), يستلم yistlim (he receives)

ex_en: When do you get paid? At the end of the month
note: imperfect: نقبض nugbuD (I get paid), يقبض yugbuD (he gets paid). ق = g. Also 'to arrest': قبضوا عليه.

ex_en: Lift the box with me
note: imperfect: نرفع nirfa3 (I lift), يرفع yirfa3 (he lifts)

ex_en: We gathered money for the wedding
note: imperfect: نجمع nijma3 (I collect), يجمع yijma3 (he collects). Intensive جمّع jamma3 also common.

ex_en: Hand out the sweets to the kids
note: imperfect: نفرّق nfarrig (I distribute), يفرّق yfarrig (he distributes). ق = g.

ex_en: Count the money before you leave
note: imperfect: نعد n3idd (I count), يعد y3idd (he counts)

ex_en: They dug a well on the farm
note: imperfect: نحفر ni7fir (I dig), يحفر yi7fir (he digs)

ex_en: We planted olives in the garden
note: imperfect: نزرع nizra3 (I plant), يزرع yizra3 (he plants). جنان jnān = garden/orchard.

ex_en: We painted the house white
note: imperfect: ندهن nidhan (I paint), يدهن yidhan (he paints)

ex_en: Stick the paper on the door
note: imperfect: نلصق nilSag (I stick), يلصق yilSag (he sticks). ق = g.

ex_en: Measure the table before buying it
note: imperfect: نقيس ngīs (I measure), يقيس ygīs (he measures). Also 'to try on': قيس القميجة.

ex_en: I registered at the university
note: imperfect: نسجّل nsajjil (I register), يسجّل ysajjil (he registers)

ex_en: Turn on the AC, it's hot
note: imperfect: نشغّل nshaghghil (I turn on), يشغّل yshaghghil (he turns on). كليماتيزور = air conditioner (French climatiseur).

ex_en: She sewed a dress for her daughter
note: imperfect: نخيّط nkhayyiT (I sew), يخيّط ykhayyiT (he sews)

ex_en: He earns good money from trade
note: imperfect: نكسب niksib (I earn), يكسب yiksib (he earns)

ex_en: Don't be late for work
note: imperfect: نتأخّر nit'akhkhar (I am late), يتأخّر yit'akhkhar (he is late)

ex_en: He quit smoking two years ago
note: imperfect: نبطّل nbaTTil (I stop), يبطّل ybaTTil (he stops)

ex_en: In Souq al-Turk you have to haggle
note: imperfect: نساوم nsāwim (I bargain), يساوم ysāwim (he bargains). Souq al-Turk = old market in Tripoli.

ex_en: I went to the bank to withdraw money
note: imperfect: نسحب nis7ab (I withdraw), يسحب yis7ab (he withdraws)

ex_en: I downloaded the app on my phone
note: imperfect: نحمّل n7ammil (I load), يحمّل y7ammil (he loads)

ex_en: Knock on the door before you go in
note: imperfect: ندق ndugg (I knock), يدق ydugg (he knocks). Also 'to call (phone)': دقّلي duggli. ق = g.

ex_en: Hello, how are you all?
note: The standard greeting; reply وعليكم السلام.

en: and upon you peace (reply to hello)
ex_en: And peace upon you, welcome.
note: Always the reply to السلام عليكم.

ex_en: Hi, how are things?
Welcome, please sit down.

en: welcome to you; nice to see you
ex_en: Welcome, you've brightened the house.
note: Plural: أهلا بيكم ahlan bīkum.

ex_en: Hi brother, where have you been?
Hello, how are you?
Welcome to Libya!
note: Very common Libyan way of welcoming a guest; the guest often replies with the same phrase.

ex_en: Hey, welcome, come on in!
How are you today?
note: Plural: كيف حالكم kīf 7ālkum.

en: how are things? (lit. what are your conditions)
ex_ar: شن حوالك؟ إن شاء الله باهي.
ex_en: How are things? Hopefully good.
note: Typically Libyan; شن shin = what.

en: what's new? how are you? (lit. what's your news)
ex_ar: شن أخبارك؟ من زمان ما شفتك.
ex_tr: shin akhbārik? min zamān ma shuftik.
ex_en: What's new? I haven't seen you in ages.
What's up, guys?
note: Casual, especially among young people; jaww literally = atmosphere/weather.

en: how are your affairs? how's everything?
ex_en: How's everything at work?

en: how's your health? how are you keeping?
ex_en: How's your health, sir?
note: Polite, especially to older people.

ex_en: How's the family? Are they well?
Fine, thank God.
note: Used both as question (لاباس؟ are you OK?) and answer.

en: are you well? (lit. no harm on you)
ex_en: Are you OK? You look tired.
I'm fine thank God, and you?
note: The standard answer to كيف حالك.

ex_en: How are you? – Good, thank God.
note: bāhi is the key Libyan word for good/OK.

ex_en: Everything OK? – All good.
Good morning, mum.
note: Reply: صباح النور.

en: good morning (reply; lit. morning of light)
ex_en: Good morning! – Good morning to you.
Good evening, how was your day?
note: Reply: مساء النور.

ex_en: Good evening! – Good evening to you.

en: good night (lit. may you wake up well)
ex_en: I'm going to sleep, good night.
note: To a woman: تصبحي على خير tiSb7i; reply: وانت من أهله.

en: and you too (reply to good night)
ex_ar: تصبح على خير! – وانت من أهله.
ex_en: Good night! – You too.
Bye, say hi to the family for me.
note: Very common Libyan goodbye; reply الله يسلمك.

ex_en: Goodbye, see you tomorrow.

en: God keep you safe (reply to goodbye)
ex_en: Bye! – Take care.
note: Also used to thank someone who wished you well.

ex_en: OK then, goodbye.
I'm busy now, see you later.
See you at the café this afternoon.
note: From تلاقى tlāga, imperfect: نتلاقى nitlāga.

en: welcome back; glad you arrived safely
ex_ar: حمد الله على السلامة! كيف كانت السفرة؟
ex_en: Welcome back! How was the trip?
note: Said to someone returning from travel, hospital, etc. Reply: الله يسلمك.

en: where have you been? long time no see
ex_en: Where have you been, man?
Long time no see! What's new?

en: where are you? where have you been?
ex_en: Where have you been? We don't see you anymore.
note: Also the usual opening on the phone.

ex_en: I missed you so much, brother!
note: Maghrebi verb توحش twa77ash 'to miss'; imperfect يتوحش yitwa77ash.

ex_en: Say hi to your mother for me.
note: Reply: يوصل yūSil (it will reach) or الله يسلمك.

en: will do (reply to 'say hi for me'; lit. it will arrive)
ex_ar: سلملي على خوك! – يوصل إن شاء الله.
ex_en: Say hi to your brother! – Will do.

en: you've brightened the place; welcome (to a guest)
ex_en: Welcome sir, please come in.
note: Reply: منور بأهله mnawwar b-ahla (it's bright thanks to its owners).

en: it's bright thanks to its people (reply to نورت)
ex_en: Welcome! – Thanks, it's your company that brightens it.
Hello, who's speaking?
note: From French allô.

ex_en: Thanks for the help.

ex_ar: صحيت يا خوي، والله ما قصرت.
ex_tr: Sa77ēt ya khūy, wallahi ma gaSSart.
ex_en: Thanks brother, you really did your best.
note: Very Libyan way of saying thanks (lit. 'you became healthy'). To a group: صحيتوا Sa77ētu.

ex_en: Thanks for the gift.
note: To a woman: مشكورة mashkūra.

en: thank you; well done (lit. may God give you health)
ex_en: Thanks for the meal.
note: Said to someone who worked hard or did you a favour.

ex_en: Thanks! – You're welcome.
Thanks! – Don't mention it.

en: please (lit. may God keep you well)
ex_en: Please pass me the salt.
note: More typical of Morocco/Algeria; Libyans more often say بالله or يرحم والديك.

ex_en: May God give you strength.
note: In Libyan/Maghrebi speech العافية is also a euphemism for 'fire'; in polite phrases it means health.

ex_en: Please close the door.
note: The most common everyday Libyan 'please'.

en: please (lit. may God have mercy on your parents)
ex_en: Please, where is the post office?
note: Polite request, common across Libya and the Maghreb.

en: please; thank you (lit. may God keep you)
ex_en: Please, wait a bit.
I'll come tomorrow, God willing.

en: wow; how wonderful (praise, wards off envy)
ex_en: Wow, your son has grown!
note: Said when admiring someone or something to avoid the evil eye.

ex_en: God bless, a new house!
note: Similar to ما شاء الله.

en: praise be to God; thank God
ex_en: I passed the exam, thank God.

en: glory be to God; how amazing
ex_en: How amazing, it's a small world.

en: in the name of God (before starting something)
ex_en: In God's name, let's eat.
God forgive me, what kind of talk is that!

ex_ar: جدي الله يرحمه كان يحب البحر.
ex_tr: jaddi allah yir7ma kān y7ibb ilba7r.
ex_en: My late grandfather, God rest his soul, loved the sea.
note: For a woman: الله يرحمها yir7amha.

ex_en: Congratulations! – Thank you.
Sorry, I didn't mean it.
note: Also heard as سمحني sm7ni. Reply: مسامح msāme7 (forgiven).

ex_en: Sorry! – No worries, brother.
Never mind, it happens.
note: Used both to apologise and to console.

en: please; here you go; come in
ex_en: Here you go, this is your coffee.
note: To a woman: تفضلي tfaDDli; plural: تفضلوا tfaDDlu.

en: go away; go on; get out
ex_en: Get out of here!
note: Literally 'outside'. Also used to urge someone on: برا امشي!

en: let's go; come on; OK then
ex_en: Let's go, we're late.
Come on kids, home!
note: Libyans use هيا as much as يلا.

ex_en: Congratulations on passing!
note: Reply: الله يبارك فيك.

ex_en: Shall I come with you? – No problem.

en: enjoy; bon appétit; wear it in good health
ex_en: A new shirt? Enjoy it!
note: Said for food, new clothes, a haircut, a shower. Reply: الله يعطيك الصحة.

ex_en: Atchoo! – Bless you.
note: The sneezer first says الحمد لله; reply يهدينا ويهديكم الله.

ex_en: I heard you're sick, get well soon.
note: Reply: الله يسلمك.

ex_en: May God heal you and give you health.
My condolences, God rest his soul.
note: Said at funerals/mourning; reply: شكر الله سعيكم.

en: happy holidays; happy birthday (lit. every year may you be well)
ex_ar: العيد غدوة، كل عام وانت بخير.
ex_en: Eid is tomorrow, happy holidays.

ex_ar: عيدكم مبروك وكل عام وانتم بخير.
ex_en: Happy Eid and many happy returns.
Happy Ramadan to everyone.
note: Reply: الله أكرم allah akram.

ex_en: Good luck in the exam!
Good luck in your new job.
God protect you, my son.

en: it's God's will; nothing can be done
ex_en: I wanted to help you but there was nothing I could do.
note: Very common Libyan expression of resignation.

en: with pleasure; gladly (lit. on my head)
ex_en: Want tea? – Gladly!

en: gladly; right away (lit. from my eye)
ex_en: Help me please. – Gladly.

en: as you like; take your time
ex_ar: امشي على كيفك، ما فيش زربة.
ex_en: Go at your own pace, there's no rush.

en: as you wish; whatever you want
ex_ar: نمشوا توا ولا بعدين؟ – كيف ما تبي.
ex_tr: nimshu tawwa walla ba3dēn? – kīf ma tibbi.
ex_en: Shall we go now or later? – As you wish.
Take it easy, the road is busy.
Don't worry, everything's fine.
note: Careful: in Libyan قلق galag often means 'to get bored/fed up'; context decides.

ex_en: Shame on you, leave him alone!
Shame, don't say that.
I wish I could come.
You missed the plane? What a pity!
Oh my God, what happened?
Oh God, I forgot the keys!
Come on, man! Really?
Really! I couldn't believe it.
Right, you have a point.
The work is perfect.
You forgot? Doesn't matter.

en: come on, behave (lit. may God guide you)
ex_en: Come on, let your brother play.
note: Mild rebuke, often affectionate.

ex_en: I don't have time, figure it out yourself.
note: Imperative of دبر dabbar; imperfect يدبر ydabbir.

en: hopefully it's good news; I hope all is well
ex_ar: اتصلت بيك نص الليل؟ إن شاء الله خير!
ex_tr: ittaSlat bīk nuSS illēl? inshallah khēr!
ex_en: She called you at midnight? Hope all is well!

ex_ar: خير إن شاء الله، علاش جيت بدري؟
ex_en: Is everything OK? Why did you come early?
This house is very big.
note: fem. كبيرة kbīra; pl. كبار kbār.

ex_en: I have a little sister.
note: fem. صغيرة Sghīra; pl. صغار Sghār.

ex_en: The food is really good.
note: fem. باهية bāhya; pl. باهيين bāhyīn. The most typical Libyan word for 'good'; alone it means 'OK'.

ex_en: The weather today is bad.
note: fem. خايبة khāyba. Libyan/Maghrebi everyday word for bad.

ex_en: This car is ugly.
note: fem. شينة shēna; Maghrebi.

ex_en: I bought a new phone.
note: fem. جديدة jdīda; pl. جداد jdād.

ex_en: The old city in Tripoli is lovely.
note: fem. قديمة gdīma; pl. قدام gdām. For people use كبير or شايب.

ex_en: The tea is hot, careful.
note: fem. سخونة skhūna. Also used for hot weather: الجو سخون.

ex_en: I want cold water.
note: fem. باردة bārda.

ex_en: The house is warm in winter.
note: fem. دافية dāfya.

ex_en: This car is fast.
note: fem. سريعة sarī3a. 'Quickly' is often بالفيسع bilfīsa3 in Libyan.

ex_en: The internet is slow today.
note: fem. بطيئة baTī'a. Colloquially a slow person is also called ثقيل.

ex_en: This bag is heavy.
note: fem. ثقيلة thgīla; pl. ثقال thgāl.

ex_en: The tea is weak today.
note: fem. خفيفة khfīfa; خفيف الدم = funny, likeable.

ex_en: The exam was easy.
note: fem. ساهلة sāhla.

ex_en: This work is hard.
note: fem. صعيبة S3ība.

ex_en: Our neighbour is very rich.
note: fem. غنية ghaniyya; pl. أغنياء aghniyā.

ex_en: Help poor people.
note: fem. فقيرة fgīra; pl. فقرا fugra.

ex_en: Poor thing, he's very tired.
note: fem. مسكينة miskīna; pl. مساكين msākīn.

ex_en: The kitchen is clean.
note: fem. نظيفة nDHīfa.

ex_en: Your clothes are dirty, change them.
note: fem. موسخة mwassikha; pl. موسخين.

ex_en: The glass is full.
note: fem. مليانة malyāna.

ex_en: Are you free this afternoon?
note: fem. فاضية fāDya.

ex_en: Meat is expensive these days.
note: fem. غالية ghālya.

ex_en: Vegetables are cheap at the market.
note: fem. رخيصة rkhīSa.

ex_en: The sea is beautiful today.
note: fem. زينة zēna.

ex_en: The film was nice.
note: fem. حلوة 7ilwa; pl. حلوين 7ilwīn.

ex_en: A beautiful view.
note: fem. جميلة jmīla. Also used to mean 'favour': عملتلي جميل.

ex_en: My brother is very tall.
note: fem. طويلة Twīla; pl. طوال Twāl.

ex_en: The way is short from here.
note: fem. قصيرة gSīra; pl. قصار gSār.

ex_en: This cat is fat.
note: fem. سمينة smīna; pl. سمان smān.

ex_en: I became thin after the diet.
note: fem. رقيقة rgīga. Libyan/Maghrebi for slim.

ex_en: The wind is strong today.
note: fem. قوية gawiyya.

ex_en: The signal is weak here.
note: fem. ضعيفة Da3īfa; pl. ضعاف D3āf.

ex_en: These trousers are loose on me.
note: fem. واسعة wās3a.

ex_en: The alley is narrow.
note: fem. ضيقة Dayyga.

ex_en: The volume is high, turn it down a bit.
note: fem. عالية 3ālya.

ex_en: This chair is low.
note: fem. واطية wāTya.

ex_en: Have the clothes dried? – Yes, they're dry.
note: fem. ناشفة nāshfa.

ex_en: Your hair is wet.
note: fem. مبلولة mablūla.

ex_en: Coffee is bitter without sugar.
note: fem. مرة murra.

ex_en: The soup is a bit salty.
note: fem. مالحة māl7a.

ex_en: Lemon is sour.
note: fem. حامضة 7āmDa. القارص is the Libyan word for lemon.

ex_en: The harissa is very spicy.
note: fem. حارة 7ārra.

ex_en: The bread is soft.
note: fem. طرية Tariyya.

ex_en: The meat is tough, cook it more.
note: fem. قاسحة gās7a. Libyan/Tunisian.

ex_en: The fish is fresh today.
note: Invariable; from Turkish taze.

ex_en: This bread is stale.
note: fem. بايتة bāyta.

ex_en: The TV is broken.
note: fem. خاسرة khāsra. Very Libyan; in MSA خاسر means 'loser'.

ex_en: The glass is broken.
note: fem. مكسورة maksūra.

ex_en: What you say is true.
note: fem. صحيحة Sa7ī7a.

ex_en: You're wrong, it's not like that.
note: fem. غالطة ghālTa.

ex_en: My mother is sick today.
note: fem. مريضة marīDa; pl. مرضى marDa.

ex_en: I'm busy now, I'll call you later.
note: fem. مشغولة mashghūla.

ex_en: My grandfather is still alive.
note: fem. حية 7ayya.

ex_en: The phone is dead, it has no charge.
note: fem. ميتة mayyta; pl. موتى mōta. ميت بالجوع = starving.

ex_en: The shop is open until ten.
note: fem. مفتوحة maftū7a.

ex_en: The door is closed.
note: fem. مسكرة msakkra.

ex_en: I have an important meeting.
note: fem. مهمة muhimma.

ex_en: It's fine, no problem.
note: fem. عادية 3ādiyya. Very common reply meaning 'no big deal'.

ex_en: Something strange!
note: fem. غريبة gharība; pl. غرب ghurb / غربا ghurba.

ex_en: This restaurant is famous.
note: fem. مشهورة mash-hūra.

ex_en: Your daughter is smart, mashallah.
note: fem. ذكية dhkiyya.

ex_en: He's good at football.
note: fem. شاطرة shāTra; pl. شطار shuTTār.

ex_en: Don't be stupid.
note: fem. غبية ghbiyya. Can be offensive.

ex_en: Are you crazy? It's cold!
note: fem. مهبولة mahbūla; pl. مهابيل mhābīl. Maghrebi; often joking.

ex_en: I'm lazy today, I don't want to work.
note: fem. كسلانة kaslāna.

ex_en: Kids are very energetic.
note: fem. نشيطة nshīTa; pl. نشاط nshāT.

ex_en: My grandmother is very kind.
note: fem. طيبة Tayyba. In Libyan طيب as a verb also means 'to cook'.

ex_en: Libyans are generous with guests.
note: fem. كريمة karīma; pl. كرما kurama.

ex_en: Don't be stingy!
note: fem. بخيلة bkhīla. Also شحيح sh7ī7.

ex_en: He's an honest man.
note: fem. صادقة Sādga.

ex_en: Don't believe him, he's a liar.
note: fem. كذابة kadhdhāba.

ex_en: Your son is well-mannered, mashallah.
note: fem. مربية mrabbya. Opposite: قليل الترباية.

ex_en: The neighbourhood is quiet at night.
note: fem. هادية hādya.

ex_en: Why are you quiet today?
note: fem. ساكتة sākta.

ex_en: This road is dangerous at night.
note: fem. خطيرة khTīra. Young people use it for 'amazing'.

ex_en: The food here is excellent.
note: fem. ممتازة mumtāza.

ex_en: The wedding was great.
note: fem. هايلة hāyla.

ex_en: I stayed home the whole day.
note: fem. كاملة kāmla.

ex_en: The bill is a dinar short.
note: fem. ناقصة nāgSa.

ex_en: Lunch is ready, come!
note: fem. جاهزة jāhza. Libyans also say واجد wājid for 'ready'.

ex_en: Is this watch genuine?
note: fem. أصلية aSliyya.

ex_en: This story is real.
note: fem. حقيقية 7agīgiyya.

ex_en: Is it clear?
note: fem. واضحة wāD7a.

ex_en: The table is round.
note: fem. مدورة mdawwra.

ex_en: This book is thick.
note: fem. عريضة 3rīDa.

ex_en: The wall is thick.
note: fem. غليظة ghlīDHa.

ex_en: The sea is deep here, be careful.
note: fem. عميقة 3mīga.

ex_en: That old man is our neighbour.
note: fem. شايبة shāyba; pl. شيابين shyābīn. Also noun: old man.

ex_en: Your friend is charming.
note: fem. ظريفة DHrīfa.

ex_en: The film was very funny.
note: fem. مضحكة muD7ka.

ex_en: Silly talk.
note: fem. سخيفة sakhīfa.

ex_en: Sorry, I'm in a hurry.
note: fem. مستعجلة mista3jla. Libyans also say عندي زربة 'I'm in a rush'.

ex_en: Smoking is forbidden here.
note: fem. ممنوعة mamnū3a.

ex_en: Is entry allowed?
note: fem. مسموحة masmū7a.

ex_en: You're free, do what you want.
note: fem. حرة 7urra; pl. أحرار a7rār.

ex_en: Is dinner ready?
note: Libyan usage (in the Gulf واجد means 'a lot'). fem. واجدة wājda.

ex_en: I'm very happy for you.
note: fem. فرحانة far7āna; pl. فرحانين.

ex_en: Are you happy in your job?
note: fem. مبسوطة mabsūTa.

ex_en: I'm relaxed now after the holiday.
note: fem. مرتاحة mirtā7a. Can also mean 'well-off'.

en: in a good mood; chilled out
ex_en: I'm in a good mood today, I want to go out.
note: fem. رايقة rāyga.

ex_en: Why are you sad? What happened?
note: fem. حزينة 7zīna.

ex_en: She's upset by what he said.
note: fem. مقهورة magh-hūra. Very common in Libyan for emotional hurt; ق is pronounced g here.

ex_en: You look down today.
note: fem. مغبونة maghbūna. Libyan/Tunisian; noun غبنة ghubna = sorrow.

ex_en: My brother is upset with me.
note: fem. زعلانة za3lāna.

ex_en: My dad is angry, don't talk to him now.
note: fem. متغششة mitghashsha. Very Libyan; verb تغشش tghashshash, imperfect يتغشش yitghashshash.

ex_en: Why are you so worked up?
note: fem. معصبة m3aSSba.

ex_en: I'm tired, I'll sleep early.
note: fem. تعبانة ta3bāna. Can also mean 'unwell'.

ex_en: After work I'm worn out.
note: fem. مهدودة mahdūda.

ex_en: I'm sleepy, I didn't sleep last night.
note: fem. ناعسة nā3sa.

ex_en: I'm bored at home, I want to go out.
note: fem. قلقانة galgāna. False friend: in Libyan it mainly means bored, not 'worried' as in MSA قلقان.

ex_en: The little one is scared of the dog.
note: fem. خايفة khāyfa.

ex_en: I woke up startled by the noise.
note: fem. مخلوعة makhlū3a. Maghrebi/Libyan; verb تخلع tkhalla3 'to get a fright'.

ex_en: I'm worried about my mother.
note: fem. مشغولة البال. Also بالي مشغول bāli mashghūl 'I'm worried'.

ex_en: He looks troubled by debts.
note: fem. مهمومة mahmūma.

ex_en: Before exams I'm always nervous.
note: fem. متوترة mitwattra.

ex_en: I'm really under pressure this week.
note: fem. مضغوطة maDghūTa.

ex_en: I'm annoyed by the traffic.
note: fem. متضايقة mitDāyga.

ex_en: He's in love with her.
note: fem. مغرومة maghrūma. Libyan/Maghrebi.

ex_en: I've loved the sea since I was little.
note: fem. عاشقة 3āshga.

ex_en: I miss my mother a lot.
note: fem. متوحشة mitwa77sha. From توحش 'to miss'; not related to 'wild'.

ex_ar: بعد شهر في الغربة ولّيت متوحش البلاد.
ex_tr: ba3d shahr fi ilghurba wallēt mitwa77ish ilblād.
ex_en: After a month abroad I became homesick.
note: البلاد ilblād here = the homeland/home town.

ex_en: We miss you, uncle.
note: fem. مشتاقة mishtāga.

ex_en: I was embarrassed to ask him.
note: fem. محشومة ma7shūma. Libyan/Maghrebi; noun حشمة 7ashma = shame, modesty.

ex_en: My daughter is shy with people.
note: fem. خجولة khajūla.

ex_en: He's jealous of his brother.
note: fem. غيرانة ghayrāna.

ex_en: I'm surprised by what happened.
note: fem. مستغربة mistaghrba.

ex_en: I'm torn, what should I buy?
note: fem. محتارة mi7tāra.

ex_en: I'm excited for the match tonight.
note: fem. متحمسة mit7amsa.

ex_en: I'm proud of you, son.
note: fem. فخورة fakhūra.

ex_en: Are you satisfied with the work?
note: fem. راضية rāDya.

ex_en: I'm grateful to you for everything.
note: fem. ممنونة mamnūna.

ex_en: I feel lonely here.
note: fem. وحيدة wa7īda.

ex_en: My mother is very affectionate.
note: fem. حنينة 7nīna.

ex_en: The joy of Eid.
note: Also = wedding celebration in some regions.

ex_en: There's sadness in his eyes.
There are no hard feelings between us.
He said it in a moment of anger.
note: Noun related to Libyan تغشش 'to get angry'.

ex_en: Fear doesn't help.
Love can't be bought with money.
A song full of passion.
I don't hate anyone.
Life's worries never end.
note: pl. هموم hmūm.

ex_en: It needs patience.
There's still hope.
I'm not in the mood to go out.
My nerves are frayed today.
note: sg. عصب 3aSab.

en: being away from home; life abroad
ex_en: Living away from home is hard.
This man is our new neighbour.
note: pl. رجالة rjāla / رجال rjāl. راجلي rājli = my husband.

ex_en: This woman works at the hospital.
note: pl. نسوان niswān / نسا nsa. With a possessive it becomes مرت- mart-: مرتي marti = my wife.

ex_en: This child has been crying since the morning.
note: pl. أطفال aTfāl. Libyans also say صغار Sghār for 'kids'.

ex_en: The kids are playing in the house.
note: pl. صغار Sghār. Also an adjective 'small'; as a noun الصغار = the children.

ex_en: The baby is asleep, lower your voice.
note: From European 'bebè/baby'; very common in Libyan homes. Formal: رضيع raDī3.

ex_en: I have one son and two daughters.
note: pl. أولاد awlād / ولاد wlād. ولدي wildi = my son. زوز zōz = two (Libyan).

ex_ar: البنت هذي تقرا معاي في الجامعة.
ex_tr: il-bint hādhi tigra m3āy fi l-jām3a.
ex_en: This girl studies with me at university.
note: pl. بنات banāt.

ex_en: Whose little boy is this?
note: Diminutive of ولد wild. Affectionate.

ex_en: This little girl is lovely, God protect her.
note: Diminutive of بنت bint; pl. بنيّات bnayyāt.

ex_en: My friend is coming from Benghazi today.
note: pl. صحاب S7āb. Also means 'owner' (صاحب الحوش = owner of the house).

ex_en: I went with my (female) friend to the market.
note: pl. صاحبات SāHbāt.

ex_en: This is my friend from school days.
note: pl. رفاق rfāg / رفقة. ق pronounced g.

ex_en: Our neighbour is a very kind man.
note: pl. جيران jīrān.

ex_en: The neighbour brought us a plate of bazeen.
note: pl. جارات jārāt. بازين bāzīn = Libyan national dish.

ex_en: We have guests tonight.
note: pl. ضيوف Dyūf. Hospitality to ضيوف is a point of honour in Libya.

ex_en: There's a person waiting for you outside.
note: pl. أشخاص ashkhāS. In speech واحد wā7id 'someone' is also very common.

ex_en: People in Tripoli love the sea.
note: Collective noun, takes plural agreement.

ex_en: The guys went to play football.
note: Used as a friendly address: يا شباب yā shbāb = hey guys.

ex_en: This young man works at the bank.
note: pl. شباب shbāb.

ex_en: This young woman is a new doctor.
note: pl. شابات shābbāt.

ex_ar: الشيباني هذا يعرف تاريخ المدينة كله.
ex_tr: ish-shībāni hādha ya3rif tārīkh il-mdīna kullah.
ex_en: This old man knows the whole history of the city.
note: pl. شيابين shyābīn. Libyan/Maghrebi word, from شيب 'grey hair'.

ex_en: This old woman tells lovely folk tales.
note: pl. عجايز 3jāyiz. خرّافة kharrāfa = folk tale.

ex_ar: السلام عليكم يا حاج، كيف حالك؟
ex_en: Peace be upon you, sir, how are you?
note: Respectful address for any older man, pilgrimage or not. Fem. حاجة 7ājja.

ex_en: The old lady cooked soup for us.
note: Respectful address for an older woman.

ex_en: The tribal elder solved the problem.
note: pl. شيوخ shyūkh / مشايخ mashāyikh.

ex_en: The grown-ups are sitting in the guest room.
note: pl. of كبير kbīr. مربوعة marbū3a = Libyan sitting room for guests.

ex_en: The whole group came to the wedding.
note: Also 'my folks': جماعتي jmā3ti.

ex_tr: ma tiftaHsh il-bāb li ayy gharīb.
ex_en: Don't open the door to any stranger.
note: pl. غُرب ghurb / غرباء ghurabā'.

ex_ar: فيه أجانب ياسر يخدموا في الشركة.
ex_tr: fīh ajānib yāsir yikhdmu fi sh-sharika.
ex_en: Many foreigners work at the company.
note: pl. أجانب ajānib.

ex_en: I'm a Libyan from Misrata.
note: pl. ليبيين lībiyyīn; fem. ليبية lībiyya.

ex_en: This charity helps orphans.
note: pl. يتامى ytāma / أيتام aytām.

ex_en: I don't have an enemy in the world.
note: pl. أعداء a3dā'.

ex_en: May God keep your children for you.
note: Libyan/Bedouin word for one's kids; very common in blessings.

ex_ar: جدي كان بدوي يعيش في الخيمة.
ex_tr: jiddi kān badwi y3īsh fi l-khēma.
ex_en: My grandfather was a Bedouin who lived in a tent.
note: pl. بدو badu.

ex_en: Today's generation loves the phone a lot.
note: pl. أجيال ajyāl.

ex_en: My mother cooks the best couscous.
note: pl. أمهات ummahāt. Also الوالدة il-wālda (polite).

ex_en: My father works in Tripoli.
note: Libyan form: بوي būy = my father, بوك būk = your father. Also used in names/nicknames (بو بكر). pl. آباء ābā'.

ex_en: Dad brought us sweets.
note: Affectionate, used by children and adults.

ex_en: Mum, where's the key?
note: Affectionate.

ex_en: My late father was a teacher.
note: الوالدين il-wāldēn = parents. Fem. والدة wālda.

ex_en: My older brother lives in Misrata.
note: Libyan: خوي khūy = my brother. pl. خوت khūt (خوتي khūti = my brothers/siblings).

ex_en: My sister studies medicine.
note: pl. خوات khwāt.

ex_en: My (paternal) uncle is coming to have lunch with us.
note: pl. عمام 3mām. A wife may also call her father-in-law عمي 3ammi.

ex_en: My paternal aunt lives near us.
note: pl. عمات 3ammāt.

ex_en: My maternal uncle has a house in the countryside.
note: pl. خوال khwāl.

ex_en: My maternal aunt brought a present for the baby.
note: pl. خالات khālāt.

ex_en: My grandfather is ninety years old.
note: pl. جدود jdūd (also 'ancestors').

ex_en: My grandmother tells us folk tales.
note: pl. جدات jiddāt. See also حنّا 7anna.

ex_en: Granny made us asida.
note: Libyan affectionate word for grandmother (حنّي 7anni = my granny). عصيدة 3aSīda = traditional porridge.

ex_en: My cousin (paternal uncle's son) lives in Benghazi.
note: pl. ولاد عم wlād 3amm. Also used loosely for close kin/tribe.

ex_ar: بنت عمي تعرّست الصيف اللي فات.
ex_en: My cousin got married last summer.
note: pl. بنات عم banāt 3amm.

ex_en: My cousin (maternal uncle's son) works with me.
note: pl. ولاد خال wlād khāl.

ex_ar: بنت خالي تقرا في كلية الهندسة.
ex_tr: bint khāli tigra fi kulliyyit il-handasa.
ex_en: My cousin studies in the engineering faculty.
note: pl. بنات خال banāt khāl.

ex_en: My cousin (maternal aunt's son) is coming to visit us.
note: Arabic distinguishes cousins by which parent's sibling they come from.

ex_en: Her husband works abroad.
note: Formal-ish; in daily speech راجلها rājilha 'her man' is more common. Careful: زوز zōz = 'two'.

ex_en: His wife is a dentist.
note: Daily speech prefers مرته martah 'his woman' or حرمته 7urmtah.

ex_en: Give my regards to your wife and kids.
note: Polite, indirect way to refer to someone's wife.

ex_en: My family is big, I have seven siblings.
note: pl. عايلات 3āylāt. Also pronounced عيلة 3ēla.

ex_ar: نبي نمشي نزور أهلي في العيد.
ex_tr: nibbi nimshi nzūr ahli fi l-3īd.
ex_en: I want to go visit my family for Eid.
note: أهل الحوش = the household.

ex_en: All the relatives came to the funeral gathering.
note: sg. قريب grīb. ق pronounced g.

ex_ar: كل واحد في ليبيا يعرف قبيلته.
ex_tr: kull wā7id fi lībya ya3rif gbīltah.
ex_en: Everyone in Libya knows their tribe.
note: pl. قبايل gbāyil. Tribal ties remain important in Libyan social life.

ex_en: My in-law is a respectable man.
note: pl. نسابة nsāba. Covers male in-laws broadly.

ex_en: My mother-in-law loves me a lot.
note: Also called خالتي khālti or عمتي 3ammti out of politeness.

ex_en: The bride is wearing a traditional wrap and Libyan jewellery.
note: pl. عرايس 3rāyis. Also used for a doll and for a sandwich (عروسة تن).

ex_en: The groom came in the decorated car.
note: pl. عرسان 3irsān. عرس 3irs = wedding.

ex_en: Her fiancé works as an engineer.
note: Fem. خطيبة khTība = fiancée.

ex_en: I brought a present for my fiancée.
note: خطوبة khTūba = engagement.

ex_en: The old man has twenty grandchildren.
note: pl. أحفاد a7fād / حفدة.

ex_en: I named my first granddaughter after my mother.
note: pl. حفيدات 7fīdāt.

ex_ar: الأرملة هذي تربي في أربع صغار.
ex_tr: il-armla hādhi trabbi fi arba3 Sghār.
ex_en: This widow is raising four kids.
note: pl. أرامل arāmil. Masc. أرمل armal.

ex_en: These kids are twins.
note: Also heard as توام twām in Maghrebi speech.

ex_en: How many siblings do you have?
note: pl. of خو khū. Libyan form.

ex_en: My head has been hurting since morning.
note: pl. روس rūs / ريوس ryūs.

ex_en: Her eyes are blue.
note: dual عينين 3aynēn; pl. عيون 3yūn.

ex_en: Wash your hands before eating.
note: dual يدّين yiddēn (used as plural).

ex_en: My foot hurts from walking.
note: dual رجلين rijlēn. Also كراع kurā3 for 'leg' in Maghrebi speech.

ex_en: He's kind-hearted.
note: pl. قلوب glūb. ق pronounced g.

ex_en: Her hair is long and black.
note: Collective; one hair = شعرة sha3ra. أكحل ak7al = black (Libyan).

ex_en: Close your mouth while you eat.
note: pl. أفواه afwāh.

ex_en: I have a tooth that hurts.
note: pl. سنون snūn / أسنان asnān.

ex_en: My wisdom tooth came through.
note: pl. ضروس Drūs.

ex_en: My nose is blocked from the cold.
note: pl. خشوم khshūm. Libyan word; MSA أنف is not used in daily speech.

ex_en: My ear hurts.
note: dual وذنين widhnēn; pl. وذان wdhān.

ex_en: Wash your face and come.
note: pl. وجوه wjūh.

ex_en: He has a sharp tongue (lit. long tongue).
note: pl. ألسنة alsina.

ex_en: My lips are chapped from the cold.
note: pl. شفايف shfāyif.

ex_en: She kissed her on the cheek.
note: pl. خدود khdūd.

ex_en: Put your hand on his forehead, he's hot.
note: pl. جباه jbāh.

ex_en: Her eyebrows are thin.
note: pl. حواجب 7wājib.

ex_en: His eyelashes are long.
note: pl. رموش rmūsh.

ex_en: My father has a white beard.
note: pl. لحى li7a.

ex_en: He grew a moustache like his grandfather.
note: sg. شارب shārib; the plural is used for one moustache.

ex_en: My neck hurts from the pillow.
note: pl. رقاب rgāb.

ex_en: My throat is burning.
note: pl. حلوق 7lūg.

ex_en: I carried the bag on my shoulder.
note: pl. كتاف ktāf.

ex_en: He broke his arm in the match.
note: pl. ذرعان dhir3ān.

ex_en: I hit my elbow on the door.
note: pl. كيعان kī3ān.

ex_en: I cut my finger with the knife.
note: pl. صوابع Swāba3.

ex_en: Cut your nails.
note: pl. ظوافر DHwāfir.

ex_en: My back hurts from work.
note: pl. ظهور DHhūr.

ex_en: He has a pain in his chest.
note: pl. صدور Sdūr.

ex_en: My stomach hurts, I ate too much.
note: pl. كروش krūsh. The everyday Libyan word for tummy.

ex_en: He has a stomach problem.
note: More medical/formal than كرش karsh.

ex_en: He slept on his stomach.
note: pl. بطون bTūn.

ex_en: The baby's navel stump hasn't fallen off yet.
note: pl. سرر Surar.

ex_en: I fell and grazed my knee.
note: pl. ركب rukab.

ex_en: He has a torn thigh muscle.
note: pl. فخاذ fkhādh.

ex_ar: كعبي يوجع فيا من الصباط الجديد.
ex_tr: ka3bi yūja3 fiyya min iS-SabbāT il-jdīd.
ex_en: My heel hurts from the new shoes.
note: pl. كعوب k3ūb. Also 'heel of a shoe'.

ex_en: You need to look after your body.
note: pl. أجسام ajsām.

ex_en: My skin is dry in winter.
note: pl. جلود jlūd.

ex_en: Blood came out of his nose.
note: pl. دماء dimā'.

ex_en: A bone in his leg broke.
note: pl. عظام 3DHām; one bone = عظمة 3aDHma.

ex_en: Use your brain!
note: pl. مخاخ mkhākh.

ex_en: He has a liver disease.
note: Also used affectionately: يا كبدتي yā kibdti 'my darling'.

ex_en: He had a kidney operation.
note: pl. كلاوي klāwi.

ex_en: Smoking harms the lungs.
note: pl. ريات riyyāt.

ex_en: He has an intestinal inflammation.
note: sg. مصران muSrān.

ex_en: I saw tears in his eyes.
note: sg. دمعة dam3a.

ex_en: He has a bruise on his shin.
note: pl. سيقان sīgān.

ex_en: She read his palm.
note: pl. كفوف kfūf. Also 'slap': عطاه كف = he slapped him.

ex_en: You need to go to the doctor today.
note: pl. دكاترة dakātra. Fem. دكتورة doktōra. The everyday word; طبيب Tbīb is more formal.

ex_en: The physician told me to rest for a week.
note: pl. أطباء aTibbā'. جمعة jum3a = week (Libyan).

ex_en: Take the medicine after eating.
note: pl. أدوية adwiya.

ex_en: Is there a pharmacy open tonight?
note: pl. صيدليات Saydaliyyāt.

ex_en: They took him to the hospital by ambulance.
note: From Italian ospedale (via Maghrebi). pl. سبيطارات sbīTārāt. مستشفى mustashfa is also used.

ex_en: Tripoli Central Hospital is big.
note: pl. مستشفيات mustashfayāt. Used in official names.

ex_en: The clinic opens at nine.
note: pl. عيادات 3yādāt. Private clinics are very common in Libya.

ex_en: The little one has had a fever since yesterday.
note: Libyan/Maghrebi, from سخون skhūn 'hot'. MSA حمّى 7umma.

ex_en: I caught a cold from the chilly weather.
note: Also خذاني البرد khdhāni l-bard 'the cold got me'.

ex_en: Be careful you don't catch a cold.
note: Also means 'cold weather'.

ex_en: He has a cough that won't go away.
note: Verb: يكح yku77.

ex_en: I have a pain in my back.
note: pl. أوجاع awjā3. Verb يوجع yūja3: راسي يوجع فيا = my head hurts.

ex_en: I have a headache from the noise.
note: Also صداع Sudā3 (more formal).

ex_en: He has a migraine.
note: صداع نصفي = migraine.

ex_en: This wound needs stitches.
note: pl. جروح jrū7.

ex_en: The injury to his knee is minor.
note: pl. إصابات iSābāt.

ex_en: He has a fracture in his arm.
note: pl. كسور ksūr.

ex_en: They put a cast on him for a month.
note: Lit. 'gypsum'.

ex_en: This illness is contagious.
note: pl. أمراض amrāD.

ex_en: The patient is waiting for the doctor.
note: pl. مرضى marDa. Also adjective 'sick'.

ex_ar: خوذ حبة الصبح وحبة في الليل.
ex_en: Take one pill in the morning and one at night.
note: pl. حبوب 7būb. Also 'a grain/piece'.

ex_en: The little one is afraid of injections.
note: pl. إبر ibar.

ex_en: The doctor ordered a blood test.
note: pl. تحاليل ta7ālīl.

ex_en: The nurse gave me the injection.
note: pl. ممرضات. Masc. ممرض mumarriD.

ex_en: Call the ambulance quickly!
note: سيارة إسعاف = ambulance.

ex_en: My father had heart surgery.
note: pl. عمليات 3amaliyyāt.

ex_en: My grandfather has diabetes.
note: In speech diabetes is simply السكر 'the sugar'.

ex_ar: خالي عنده الضغط، ما ياكلش ملح.
ex_en: My uncle has high blood pressure, he doesn't eat salt.
note: عنده الضغط = he has hypertension.

ex_en: I have a dust allergy.
note: pl. حساسيات.

ex_en: He went abroad for treatment; the treatment is expensive.
note: Many Libyans travel to Tunisia for علاج.

ex_en: Health is the most important thing.
note: صحة! Sa77a = 'bless you / enjoy' (said after eating or a haircut).

ex_en: Take his temperature, he looks hot.
note: Also weather heat.

ex_en: I got dizzy while standing.
note: Verb: داخ dākh 'to get dizzy'.

ex_ar: الصغير عنده إسهال، اعطيه ما ياسر.
ex_en: The little one has diarrhoea, give him lots of water.
I have an itch on my hand.
note: Verb: يحك y7ukk.

ex_en: She burned her hand in the kitchen.
note: pl. حروق 7rūg.

ex_ar: فيه ورم في رجله من الضربة.
ex_tr: fīh waram fi rijlah min iD-Darba.
ex_en: There's swelling on his foot from the knock.
note: pl. أورام awrām.

ex_en: I have an appointment with the dentist.
note: Also دكتور سنون doktōr snūn.

ex_en: Kids need vaccinations before school.
note: pl. تطعيمات.

ex_en: I feel very tired today.
note: Also 'effort': تعبك ما يضيعش = your effort won't be wasted.

ex_en: His wife is in the hospital to give birth.
The pharmacist asked for the prescription.
note: pl. وصفات waSfāt. Also 'recipe'.

ex_en: Wrap the wound with gauze.
My eyesight has got weaker, I need glasses.
Put on your clothes, we're going out.
note: Lit. 'things'; Libyan everyday word for clothes. sg. حاجة 7āja 'thing'.

ex_en: This outfit suits you.
note: pl. لبسات libsāt.

ex_en: I bought a white shirt for the wedding.
note: pl. قمايج gmāyij. Maghrebi form of قميص.

ex_en: These trousers are too long for me.
note: pl. سراويل srāwīl. بنطلون banTalōn is also used.

ex_en: Take off your shoes before you come in.
note: pl. صبابيط Sbābīṭ. Maghrebi word (cf. Spanish zapato / Italian ciabatta).

ex_en: Wear your slippers in the house.
note: pl. شلايك shlāyik. Libyan/Tunisian word.

ex_en: Take the jacket, the weather's cold.
note: From Italian giacchetta / French jaquette. pl. جاكيتات.

ex_en: I wore the black coat in winter.
note: From Italian cappotto. pl. كبابيط kbābīT.

ex_en: She bought a new dress for Eid.
note: pl. فساتين fsātīn.

ex_en: This skirt is very short.
note: pl. تنانير.

ex_en: My sister wears the hijab.
note: pl. حجابات.

ex_en: She wore a black abaya.
note: pl. عبايات 3abāyāt.

ex_ar: جدتي كانت تلبس الفراشية كي تطلع.
ex_tr: jiddti kānat tilbis il-farrāshiyya kay tiTla3.
ex_en: My grandmother used to wear the farrashiya when she went out.
note: Traditional Libyan white woollen or silk wrap covering the whole body; now worn mainly by older women or at weddings.

ex_ar: العريس لابس الجرد في ليلة الحنة.
ex_tr: il-3rīs lābis il-jard fi lēlt il-7inna.
ex_en: The groom is wearing the jard on henna night.
note: Large woollen wrap draped over the shoulder; a symbol of Libyan traditional dress. pl. جرود jrūd.

ex_en: This hawli is hand-woven.
note: Libyan traditional wrap, often worn by women; similar to the jard.

ex_en: He wore the farmla over the shirt.
note: Traditional Libyan embroidered vest, part of formal men's dress. pl. فرامل frāmil.

ex_en: My father wears the kabbous on Friday.
note: Red (or black) felt cap worn with traditional dress; also called شنّة shanna.

ex_en: The red shanna is part of our ancestors' dress.
note: Synonym of كبوس kabbūs, typical of Libyan men's traditional dress. pl. شنن.

ex_en: He put on the white skullcap for prayer.
note: pl. طواقي Twāgi. ق pronounced g.

ex_en: He wore a white jubba on Eid day.
note: pl. جبب jibab.

ex_tr: libs badla u krāfaTTa li l-mgābla.
ex_en: He wore a suit and tie for the interview.
note: pl. بدل bidal. بدلة عربية = traditional Libyan outfit.

ex_en: I don't like wearing a tie.
note: From Italian cravatta.

ex_en: Wear a light T-shirt, it's hot.
note: Maghrebi word (from Italian maglia/Spanish). pl. مراويل mrāwīl.

ex_en: The kids are wearing shorts at the beach.
note: From English. pl. شورتات.

ex_en: I like wearing jeans and a shirt.
note: Often سروال جينز.

ex_en: I put on my pyjamas and went to sleep.
note: pl. بيجامات.

ex_en: My socks are torn.
note: sg. جورب jawrab.

ex_en: I put the phone in the bag.
note: pl. شنط shunaT.

ex_en: This handbag is very expensive.
note: From Italian borsa. pl. بورسات.

ex_en: I forgot my wallet at home.
note: pl. محافظ ma7āfiDH.

ex_en: Where did I put my glasses?
note: Also نظارة naDHDHāra. نظارات شمس = sunglasses.

ex_en: The trousers are loose, I need a belt.
note: pl. حزامات / أحزمة. Also seat belt.

ex_en: She wrapped the scarf around her neck.
note: pl. شيلان shīlān.

ex_en: Give me a tissue to wipe my nose.
note: pl. محارم m7ārim. Libyan/Maghrebi word.

ex_en: This ring is made of gold.
note: pl. خواتم khwātim.

ex_en: I bought her earrings for Eid.
note: pl. حلقان. Also خرص khurS in Maghrebi speech.

ex_en: She's wearing a gold chain.
note: pl. سلاسل slāsil.

ex_en: The money's in my pocket.
note: pl. جيوب jyūb.

ex_en: The bride is wearing a traditional Libyan necklace.
note: pl. قلايد glāyid.

ex_en: Come, let's have lunch at home.
note: pl. حيشان 7ēshān. In Libya حوش = the whole house (originally a courtyard house), while بيت = a room.

ex_en: The house has four rooms.
note: pl. بيوت byūt. Libyan: بيت = room (MSA 'house'). بيت النوم = bedroom.

ex_en: The old house is in the old city.
note: pl. ديار dyār. Less common than حوش in Tripoli speech.

ex_ar: ساكنين في شقة في الدور التالت.
ex_tr: sāknīn fi shigga fi d-dōr it-tālit.
ex_en: We live in an apartment on the third floor.
note: pl. شقق shigag. ق pronounced g.

ex_en: My mother is in the kitchen cooking.
note: From Italian cucina. pl. كوزينات.

ex_en: The bathroom is at the end of the hallway.
note: pl. حمامات 7ammāmāt.

ex_en: Where's the toilet, please?
note: From French/Italian. Also بيت الما bēt il-ma.

ex_en: Show the guests into the sitting room.
note: Distinctly Libyan: a (usually square) reception room near the entrance where men receive guests. pl. مرابيع mrābī3.

ex_en: We're watching TV in the living room.
note: pl. صالات Sālāt.

ex_en: The bedroom has a big window.
note: pl. بيوت النوم.

ex_en: Close the door behind you.
note: pl. بيبان bībān / أبواب abwāb.

ex_en: Open the window, it's hot.
note: pl. شبابيك shbābīk. حلّ 7all = to open (Libyan).

ex_en: The light is coming in through the small window.
note: pl. طاقات Tāgāt / طيقان. Traditional houses have small طاقات.

ex_en: The ceiling is leaking from the rain.
note: pl. سقوف sgūf. ق pronounced g.

ex_en: I hung the clothes out on the roof.
note: pl. سطوح sTū7. Flat roofs are used for drying laundry.

ex_en: Go up the stairs slowly.
note: sg. درجة daraja (one step). Also درج daraj.

ex_en: I left the key inside the house.
note: pl. مفاتيح mfātī7.

ex_en: Hang the picture on the wall.
note: pl. حيوط 7yūT.

ex_en: The floor is wet, watch out.
note: Also القاع il-gā3 'the ground'.

ex_en: I live on the second floor.
note: pl. أدوار adwār. Also 'turn': دورك dōrak = your turn.

ex_en: We drink tea on the balcony.
note: From Italian balcone. pl. بلكونات.

ex_en: Put the car in the garage.
note: From French/Italian garage.

ex_en: We bought new furniture for the house.
note: Collective noun. أثاث athāth is the formal word.

ex_en: This bed is very comfortable.
note: pl. سرارير srārīr / أسرّة.

ex_en: This mattress is hard.
note: pl. مطارح mTāri7. Also floor mattresses for seating guests.

ex_en: Give me another pillow.
note: pl. مخاد mkhādd.

ex_en: It's a cold night, bring a blanket.
note: pl. بطاطين bTāTīn.

ex_en: Put the plates on the table.
note: From Italian tavola. pl. طاولات Tāwlāt.

ex_en: Sit on the chair.
note: pl. كراسي krāsi.

ex_en: He fell asleep on the sofa in the living room.
note: pl. كنبات.

ex_en: The clothes are in the wardrobe.
note: pl. دواليب dwālīb.

ex_en: The books are on the shelf.
note: pl. رفوف rfūf.

ex_en: He looked at himself in the mirror.
note: pl. مرايات mrāyāt.

ex_en: Close the curtain, the sun is strong.
note: pl. ستاير stāyir.

ex_en: The cold water is in the fridge.
note: pl. ثلاجات.

ex_en: Turn on the TV, there's a match.
note: pl. تلفزيونات.

ex_en: Put the clothes in the washing machine.
note: pl. غسالات.

ex_en: The AC is broken and it's hot.
note: pl. مكيفات. A wall unit is often called سبليت splīt.

ex_en: Turn on the heater, it's very cold.
note: pl. دفايات.

ex_en: A fan isn't enough in summer.
note: pl. مراوح mrāwi7.

ex_en: Put the cake in the oven.
note: pl. أفران afrān.

ex_en: The power has been out since morning.
note: Libyan: الضو = the electricity supply as well as light. pl. أضواء aDwā'.

ex_en: The bulb has burnt out, change it.
note: From Italian lampada. pl. لمبات.

ex_en: The charger is in the socket.
note: From Italian presa. pl. بريزات.

ex_en: This carpet is handmade.
note: pl. سجاجيد sjājīd. Also 'prayer rug'.

ex_ar: الكليم هذا جابته جدتي من الجبل.
ex_tr: il-klīm hādha jābitah jiddti min ij-jbal.
ex_en: My grandmother brought this kilim from the mountains.
note: pl. كلايم klāyim. Traditional Libyan woven rug.

ex_en: We removed the carpet and put down marble.
note: From French moquette.

ex_en: The tap drips all night.
note: pl. حنفيات.

ex_en: I want to take a shower.
note: From French douche.

ex_en: Give me a towel to dry off with.
note: pl. فوط fuwaT.

ex_en: Wash your hands with soap.
note: A bar = صابونة Sābūna.

ex_en: Bring the broom, let's clean the house.
note: pl. مكانس mkānis.

ex_en: Fill the bucket with water.
note: pl. سطول sTūl.

ex_en: Take the rubbish out.
note: Libyan/Maghrebi word. Bin = صندوق الزبلة.

ex_en: The iron is hot, be careful.
note: pl. مكاوي mkāwi.

ex_en: The tank on the roof is empty.
note: pl. خزانات. Many Libyan homes store water in roof tanks.

ex_en: Someone rang the doorbell.
note: pl. أجراس ajrās.

ex_en: The iron gate needs painting.
note: pl. بوابات.

ex_en: Light a candle, the power's out.
note: pl. شموع shmū3.

ex_en: Put the teapot on the fire.
note: pl. برارد brārid / برادات. Central to Libyan tea (شاهي) culture.

ex_en: Give me a glass of water.
note: pl. كيسان kīsān / كاسات.

ex_en: I washed the dishes after lunch.
note: pl. صحون S7ūn.

ex_en: The big pot is for feasts.
note: pl. طناجر Tnājir. Maghrebi word.

ex_en: Careful, the knife is sharp.
note: pl. سكاكين skākīn.

ex_en: Apartment rent is expensive in Tripoli.
note: Verb: كرى kra 'to rent'.

ex_en: The whole house floor is marble.
note: Collective noun; one slab = رخامة.

ex_en: Bring a loaf of bread from the bakery with you.
note: Libyans usually say خبزة for bread in general; pl. خبز khubz. Often bought fresh twice a day.

en: tannūr bread (flatbread baked in a clay oven)
ex_ar: خبزة التنور مع الزيت حاجة باهية.
ex_en: Tannūr bread with olive oil is a lovely thing.
note: Traditional round flatbread baked on the walls of a clay tannūr, common in homes and rural areas.

ex_en: Today we're cooking rice with fish.
note: Also pronounced rozz. Libyan 'rice with fish' (رز بالحوت) is a classic coastal dish.

ex_en: Meat has become expensive these days.
note: Libyan pronunciation inserts a vowel: la7am. Without qualification it usually means lamb/mutton.

ex_en: I want a kilo of minced meat for the mbaṭṭan.

ex_ar: لحم العلوش أحسن من لحم البقري.
ex_tr: la7am il-3allūsh a7san min la7am il-bagri.
ex_en: Lamb is better than beef.
note: علوش 3allūsh = young sheep/lamb in Libyan; lamb is the prestige meat.

ex_en: Beef is a bit cheaper.

ex_ar: في الجنوب ياكلوا لحم الجمل هلبة.
ex_tr: fi j-janūb yāklu la7am ij-jmal hallba.
ex_en: In the south they eat camel meat a lot.
note: Camel meat is sold at specialised butchers and is popular in winter.

ex_ar: أمي تدير القديد بعد العيد الكبير.
ex_tr: ummi tdīr il-gadīd ba3d il-3īd il-kbīr.
ex_en: My mother makes dried meat after Eid al-Adha.
note: Strips of sacrificial lamb salted, spiced and sun-dried; later cooked in sharba or with couscous.

ex_en: Dinner tonight is chicken in the oven.
note: Single bird: دجاجة djāja.

ex_en: The fish is fresh in the market today.
note: In Libya حوت means any fish (not 'whale' as in MSA). pl. حيتان 7ītān.

ex_en: Put tuna in the sandwich.
note: Tuna is a staple filling with harīsa and olives.

ex_en: Fried sardines are cheap and tasty.
note: From Italian sardina.

ex_en: I want two fried eggs for breakfast.
note: Very Libyan word; collective/pl. دحي da7i. MSA بيض is understood but not used.

ex_en: Our breakfast is bread, cheese and olives.
Put a little butter on the bread.
3aSīda is eaten with ghee and honey.
Mountain honey is pricey but worth it.
I went to the market to buy vegetables.
note: Collective noun used for all vegetables.

ex_en: After lunch we eat some fruit.
Tomatoes are the basis of every Libyan dish.
note: Single: حبة طماطم 7abbat TmāTim.

ex_en: Chop the onion thinly.
note: Single: بصلة bSala.

ex_en: The soup needs a little garlic.
note: A clove: سنة ثوم sinnit thūm.

ex_en: I want fried potatoes with the chicken.
note: Libyans say بطاطا, not Egyptian بطاطس.

ex_en: Put the carrots and potatoes in the stew.
note: Maghrebi word for carrots; جزر jazar is also understood.

ex_en: Hot pepper burns.
note: فلفل أخضر green pepper; فلفل حار hot pepper; فلفل أكحل black pepper.

ex_en: Add a little black pepper.
note: أكحل ak7al is the Libyan word for black.

ex_en: The salad has cucumber and tomato.
Stuffed eggplant is very tasty.
We're making stuffed zucchini today.
note: Libyan قرعة / قرع gar3 = zucchini, not Egyptian كوسة. Same word also means 'bottle'.

ex_en: Stew with beans is a summer dish.

ex_ar: الفول المدمس فطور باهي في الشتا.
ex_en: Stewed fava beans are a good winter breakfast.
Libyan soup has chickpeas in it.
Lentil soup is warming in the cold.
Put the salad on the table.
note: From Italian insalata.

ex_en: Chop some parsley over the salad.
note: Maghrebi form; Levantine بقدونس is not used.

ex_en: Fresh coriander gives a nice aroma.
Mint tea, please.
note: Fresh mint is often added to green tea.

ex_en: Apples are expensive this year.
note: Single: تفاحة tiffā7a.

ex_en: Orange juice is fresh and healthy.
note: Libyan has n at the end: برتقان, not برتقال. Single: برتقانة.

ex_en: Kids love bananas.
note: Single: موزة mūza.

ex_en: The grapes of Gharyan are famous.
In Ramadan we break the fast with dates and milk.
note: Libya grows many date varieties.

ex_en: Pomegranates come in autumn.
Watermelon in summer cools you down.
note: Maghrebi word; Libyans do not use بطيخ for watermelon.

ex_en: Fresh figs can't be passed up.
note: Maghrebi word for figs; MSA تين is rarely heard.

ex_en: The peaches are sweet this year.
Apricot jam at breakfast.
Black olives with the cheese.
Squeeze a bit of lemon on the fish.
Strawberry milkshake.
note: From Italian fragola.

ex_en: On Fridays we eat couscous.
note: Libyan couscous is usually served with lamb, chickpeas, potatoes and a spicy tomato sauce, often topped with an onion-raisin sauce (بصلة).

en: bazin (barley dough dome served with sauce)
ex_ar: البازين ياكلوه باليد في قصعة وحدة.
ex_tr: il-bāzīn yāklūh bil-yadd fi gaS3a wa7da.
ex_en: Bazin is eaten by hand from one shared bowl.
note: National dish: a dome of barley flour dough surrounded by lamb, eggs and potato in a spicy tomato sauce.

ex_en: I don't have time, I'll make mbakbka.
note: Pasta cooked directly in a spicy tomato-meat sauce; name imitates the 'bak-bak' bubbling sound.

ex_ar: في رمضان الشربة ما تغيبش على السفرة.
ex_tr: fi ramaDān ish-sharba ma tghībsh 3ala is-sufra.
ex_en: In Ramadan sharba never misses from the table.
note: شربة ليبية: tomato-lamb soup with orzo (lsān 3aSfūr), chickpeas and mint; essential at iftar.

ex_ar: في المولد يديروا العصيدة بالرب والسمن.
ex_en: For the Prophet's birthday they make 3aSīda with date syrup and ghee.
note: Also served to celebrate a new baby. رب rubb = date syrup.

ex_en: 3uSbān is an Eid al-Adha dish.
note: Tripe/intestine stuffed with rice, meat, herbs and spices; cooked in sauce or with couscous.

ex_en: The kids want pasta every day.
note: Italian legacy (maccheroni); pasta is daily food in Libya.

en: baked pasta with meat and egg
ex_en: I made baked pasta for the guests.
Rishta with chicken is a light dish.
note: Steamed noodles served with tomato sauce or chickpeas.

en: mbaṭṭan (fried potato slices stuffed with meat)
ex_en: Mbaṭṭan is made in Ramadan.
note: Potato slices sandwiched with spiced minced meat, dipped in egg and fried.

ex_en: Meat būrīk goes with sharba.
note: Ottoman-origin börek; fried or baked pastry with meat, cheese or potato.

ex_en: Stuffed vegetables take a long time.
7rāymi is a Tripoli dish.
note: Spicy fish stew; also cooked with lamb in some homes.

ex_en: Shakshuka with dried meat is a heavy breakfast.
Bsīsa with oil and sugar fills you up.
note: Roasted grains and spices ground to a flour; mixed with olive oil. Traditional travel food.

en: zummīta (roasted barley flour with oil and spices)
ex_en: My grandmother likes zummīta in the morning.
note: Similar to bsīsa; rural traditional food.

ex_en: Add more sauce to the couscous.
Put a spoonful of tomato paste in the pot.
note: From Italian salsa; in Libya it specifically means canned tomato paste.

ex_ar: الليبيين يحطوا الهريسة في كل شي.
ex_tr: il-lībiyyīn y7uTTu il-harīsa fi kull shay.
ex_en: Libyans put harissa in everything.
note: Not the Levantine semolina dessert.

ex_en: Libyan spice mix has cumin and turmeric.
note: The house blend is often called حرارات 7rārāt.

ex_en: Cumin goes with fish.
Turmeric gives rice a yellow color.
There's cinnamon on top of the 3aSīda.
Our olive oil is from the mountain.
note: Plain زيت usually means olive oil; vegetable oil is زيت نباتي or زيت قلي.

ex_en: Your tea has a lot of sugar.
The food needs a little salt.
Flour, oil and sugar from the cooperative.
note: ق → g. Barley flour for bāzīn is دقيق شعير.

ex_en: Couscous is made from semolina.
Bazin is made from barley flour.
The food is ready, come!
note: Very common Libyan/Maghrebi word for food.

ex_en: What do we have for breakfast?
note: In Ramadan فطور means the evening fast-breaking meal.

ex_en: Lunch is at three o'clock.
note: Lunch is the main meal of the day in Libya.

ex_en: Dinner is light tonight.
At suhoor we eat rice pudding.
We brought sweets for the wedding.
note: Also used as adjective 'sweet'. Pastries for occasions are called حلويات 7alawiyyāt.

ex_en: Tripolitan makrūḍ is famous at Eid.
note: Diamond-shaped semolina pastry stuffed with date paste, fried and soaked in syrup or honey.

ex_en: Ghrība melts in the mouth.
note: Made of flour/semolina, ghee and sugar; an Eid staple.

ex_en: Almond baklava is expensive.
Savory ka3k with tea.
note: Libyan ka3k comes sweet or salted (with fennel/nigella).

ex_en: Sfinz with egg in the morning.
note: Fried ring of dough, eaten plain, with sugar/honey, or with an egg fried inside.

ex_en: Zlābya is the Ramadan sweet.

ex_ar: العصيدة ما تحلاش من غير رب.
ex_tr: il-3aSīda ma ti7lāsh min ghēr rubb.
ex_en: 3aSīda isn't good without date syrup.
Bread with butter and jam.
The little one wants chocolate.
note: From Italian cioccolata.

ex_en: Put the biscuits with the tea.
We made a cake for the birthday.
Let's go eat ice cream by the sea.
note: From Italian gelato; very Libyan.

ex_en: Tea with peanuts after lunch.
note: Roasted peanuts dropped into the third glass of tea are a Libyan signature.

ex_en: Tea with almonds for guests.
note: Toasted almonds in tea are a more festive alternative to peanuts.

ex_en: I want a tuna sandwich with harissa.
note: Street sandwiches are usually in a baguette-style loaf.

ex_en: Shall we have shawarma for dinner tonight?
Pizza is everyday food in Libya.
note: Italian legacy; often pronounced with p.

ex_en: Pasta with meatballs.
Wheat and barley from the mountain.
In Zuwara the seafood is fresh.
Shrimp is very expensive.
note: From Italian gambero.

ex_en: Grilled fish with spicy salad.
The soup needs orzo.
note: Lit. 'bird's tongue'; essential in sharba lībiyya.

ex_en: Rice pudding with cinnamon.
Give me a glass of water.
note: Libyan form of ماء.

ex_ar: نشروا مية معدنية، مية الحنفية مش باهية.
ex_tr: nishru mayya ma3daniyya, mayyat il-7anafiyya mush bāhya.
ex_en: We buy bottled water; the tap water isn't good.
note: Bottled water is the norm for drinking.

ex_en: Come let's drink tea.
note: Libyans say شاهي. Tea is brewed strong, poured from height to make foam, and served in small glasses in three rounds.

ex_en: Red tea with foam.
note: Lit. 'red tea'; boiled long, very strong and sweet. Libyans call black tea 'red'.

ex_en: Green tea with mint.
The third round is tea with peanuts.
note: Usually the third, lightest round of tea.

ex_en: Tea without foam isn't worth drinking.
note: Created by pouring tea back and forth between pot and glass from a height; a mark of a skilled tea-maker.

ex_en: I only drank the first round.
note: Libyan tea comes in three rounds (first strong/bitter, second sweeter, third with peanuts). Also means a metal cup/bowl.

ex_en: I want coffee without sugar.
note: ق → g. Also means a café (coffee shop).

ex_ar: جدي يشرب القهوة العربية من الززوة.
ex_tr: jiddi yishrab il-gahwa il-3arabiyya min iz-zazwa.
ex_en: My grandfather drinks Arabic coffee from the cezve.
note: Boiled ground coffee, served in small cups.

ex_en: A macchiato, please.
note: From Italian macchiato; the signature Libyan café drink, often with lots of foam.

ex_en: The cappuccino here is good.
I want a double espresso.
Do you have instant coffee?
note: Brand name used generically.

ex_en: The milk has run out, bring a liter.
Cold buttermilk with couscous.
note: In Libya لبن is the sour drink left after churning butter, not plain milk.

ex_en: Rāyib is drunk in summer.
Strawberry yogurt for the kids.
Banana-milk juice.
note: Thick fruit-milk blends are popular at juice shops.

ex_en: Bring a cold soda.
note: From Italian gassosa.

ex_en: Fresh lāgbi in the oases.
note: Sweet sap tapped from date palms; drunk fresh in the south and oases before it ferments.

ex_en: Hot cocoa in the cold.
What drink do you want?
Put ice in the juice.
A little orange-blossom water in the coffee.
note: Added to coffee and sweets for aroma.

ex_en: Drink a herbal tea for your stomach.
Tea with extra sugar.
note: Libyan tea is typically very sweet.

ex_en: Coffee without sugar, please.
My mother is in the kitchen cooking.
note: From Italian cucina; also heard كوزينة kūzīna. MSA مطبخ is understood.

ex_en: A small cup of coffee.
note: pl. فناجين fnājīn.

ex_en: I drink milk from a mug.
Give me a spoon for the soup.
note: pl. معالق m3ālig. Note Libyan metathesis vs MSA ملعقة.

ex_en: Pasta is eaten with a fork.
note: Older speakers may say فرشيطة from Italian forchetta.

ex_en: The soup is in the pot on the fire.
note: pl. برم buram.

ex_en: Fry the eggs in the pan.
note: From Turkish tava.

ex_en: Couscous is steamed in the kaskās.
note: Perforated pot set on top of the pot of sauce.

ex_en: Put the chicken in the oven for an hour.
note: Libyan for both a home oven and the neighbourhood bakery.

ex_en: The meat is in the freezer.
Turn off the gas before you leave.
note: Also the cooking gas cylinder.

ex_en: Tea on the brazier tastes better.
Bring the tea tray.
note: pl. صواني Swāni.

ex_en: The bazin is in a big bowl.
note: Traditional wooden or metal bowl from which the family eats together.

ex_en: Give me the ladle so I can serve the soup.
Drain the pasta in the colander.
Crush the garlic in the mortar.
Make the coffee in the cezve.
note: From Turkish cezve.

ex_en: Put the water in the kettle.
The juice is in the blender.
Heat the food in the microwave.
Bring a bottle of water from the fridge.
note: Same word as zucchini; context decides. pl. قراعي grā3i.

ex_en: The jam is in the jar.
Put the lid on the pot.
A can of tomatoes and a can of tuna.
note: pl. علب 3ulab.

ex_en: Who's going to wash the dishes?
note: Libyan collective for dishes/kitchenware.

ex_en: The sponge is old, replace it.
The dishes are in the sink.

en: dining spread; table set for a meal
ex_en: The table is ready, please come.
note: Often a cloth spread on the floor for a family meal.

ex_en: Do you have matches so I can light the gas?
note: Libyan word; MSA كبريت is understood.

ex_en: The tea is in the thermos for the trip.
Give me a napkin.
note: Paper tissues are often called كلينكس by brand name.

ex_en: Chop the onion on the board.
I don't have money now.
note: Plural in form; agreement often plural (الفلوس خلصوا).

ex_en: The price is ten dinars.
note: pl. دنانير dnānīr; after numbers 3–10 Libyans often keep the singular.

ex_en: Bread used to cost fifty dirhams.
note: 1 dinar = 1000 dirhams. pl. دراهم drāhim, also used loosely for 'money'.

ex_en: He doesn't have a single penny.
note: Old unit kept in idioms.

ex_en: Do you have change for ten dinars?
Take your change.
Keep the change.
What's the price of this?
note: Maghrebi word; سعر si3r is also used, esp. in news.

ex_en: The dollar rate went up today.
note: pl. أسعار as3ār.

ex_en: How much is a kilo?
note: The basic shopping question.

ex_en: Entry is free.
note: Also means 'for nothing/in vain'. ببلاش bblāsh = for free.

ex_ar: الحانوت اللي في الزنقة يبيع كل شي.
ex_tr: il-7ānūt illi fiz-zanga ybī3 kull shay.
ex_en: The shop in the street sells everything.
note: pl. حوانيت 7wānīt.

ex_en: We go to the market on Friday.
note: ق → g. pl. أسواق aswāg. Weekly markets are named for the day (سوق الجمعة, سوق الثلاثاء).

ex_en: The new supermarket has everything.
The shop is closed on Friday.
note: pl. محلات ma7allāt.

ex_en: Let's go to the mall in the evening.
The vegetable market opens early.
Fresh fish is at the fish market.
The butcher cut the meat for me.
The baker starts work at dawn.
note: The bakery itself is الكوشة.

ex_en: This greengrocer sells at a good price.
The spices are from the spice seller.
The customer is always right.
note: pl. زبائن zbāyin.

ex_en: The merchants raised the prices.
note: pl. تجار tujjār.

ex_en: Give me the bill, please.
note: From Italian fattura.

ex_en: Take the receipt if you want to return it.
The bill is on me today.
note: Libyans often argue over who pays.

ex_en: There's a discount on the clothes.
Offer: two for the price of one.
Give me a bag for the vegetables.
note: Libyan/Maghrebi word; also a sack (e.g. of flour).

ex_en: A fifty-kilo sack of flour.
note: pl. أكياس akyās.

ex_en: Put the things in the basket.
Get a cart, there's a lot of stuff.
note: From Italian carrozza; also a horse cart or pram.

ex_en: Put the tomatoes on the scale.

ex_ar: عطيني كيلو طماطم ونص كيلو بصل.
ex_en: Give me a kilo of tomatoes and half a kilo of onions.
Two liters of milk, please.

en: piece; item; one (of a countable item)
ex_en: I want five loaves of bread.
note: Used as a counter for fruit, eggs, bread, etc.

ex_en: A pack of cigarettes and a packet of biscuits.
note: From Italian pacco.

ex_en: A carton of water has six bottles.
note: From Italian cartone.

ex_en: The queue at the bank is very long.
note: Turkish origin; queues for cash and fuel are a familiar Libyan experience.

ex_en: Payment is cash only.
The banks have no cash.
note: Common topic in Libya due to recurring banknote shortages.

ex_en: Can I pay by card?
note: ق → g.

ex_en: Pay with a certified cheque.
I buy on credit and pay at the end of the month.
note: بالدين = on credit, common at neighbourhood shops.

ex_en: Buying from the market is cheaper.
note: Verb: يشري yishri 'to buy' (Libyan/Maghrebi).

ex_en: Buying and selling.
Hard currency is hard to find.
How much is the dollar on the market?
I exchanged the dollars on the black market.
note: The parallel exchange market is a daily reference in Libya.

ex_en: The money changer is in Souq al-Mushir.
The phone has a one-year warranty.
I bought a second-hand pram for the baby.
We buy oil wholesale.
Pay at the checkout.
note: Also 'box, chest'.

ex_en: Do you have a bigger size?
note: ق → g.

ex_en: The salary hasn't come in.
note: شهرية shahriyya = monthly pay.

ex_en: What color is the car?
note: pl. ألوان alwān.

ex_en: Kids like colorful clothes.
I want the red shirt.
note: fem. حمرا 7amra; pl. حمر 7umur.

ex_en: The red rose.
Green tea.
note: fem. خضرا khaDra; pl. خضر khuDur.

ex_en: Green Square.
The sea is blue today.
note: ق → g. fem. زرقا zarga.

ex_en: Her eyes are blue and the bag is blue.
note: pl. زرق zurg.

ex_en: The taxi is yellow.
note: fem. صفرا Safra. Also 'pale' (of a face).

ex_en: The yellow flower.
He's wearing a black coat.
note: Libyan/Maghrebi word for black; أسود is understood but sounds formal. fem. كحلة ka7la.

ex_en: The black bag is mine.
note: pl. كحل ku7ul.

ex_en: The wall is white.
note: fem. بيضا bēDa; pl. بيض bīD.

ex_en: The white car is his.
The table is brown.
note: Libyans typically say قهوي for brown; بني bunni also used.

ex_en: His eyes are brown.
The car is grey.
note: Lit. 'lead-colored'; common Libyan word for grey. رمادي rmādi also used.

ex_en: The sky is grey today.
The ball is orange.
note: From برتقان burtgān (orange fruit).

ex_en: The girl wants a pink dress.
note: روز rōz (from French/Italian rosa) is also heard.

ex_en: The purple flower.
The navy suit.
The wall is sky blue.
An olive-green shirt.
The sofa is beige.
The watch is gold-colored.
The car is silver.
Her eyes are hazel.
A burgundy bag.
I want light blue.
Dark green is nicer.
note: ق → g.

ex_en: The team is wearing light blue.
A dark green door.
Her son is blond.
note: fem. شقرا shagra.

ex_en: He's tanned from the sun.
note: fem. سمرا samra.

ex_en: The wall is olive green.
The sea is turquoise in summer.
The dress is dark red.
The wall is pale yellow.
The little one draws with colors.
note: pl. of لون.

ex_en: The house is on this street.
note: pl. شوارع shwāri3

ex_en: The road is jammed today.
note: pl. طرقات Turgāt

ex_en: I go to the mosque to pray the Friday prayer.
note: pl. جوامع jwāmi3. جامع is the everyday word; مسجد is more formal.

ex_en: I went to the bank to withdraw money.
note: pl. مصارف maSārif. Libyan banks are officially called مصرف; بنك bank is also understood.

ex_en: The post office is closed today.
Call the police now!
We went to the police station to report it.
Martyrs' Square is in the center of Tripoli.
note: pl. ميادين myādīn

ex_en: I live in Tripoli.
note: Capital of Libya. Locals pronounce it Trābles (also Trāblus).

ex_en: My brother works in Benghazi.
note: Libya's second city, capital of the east (Barga).

ex_en: Misrata is famous for trade.
note: Port city east of Tripoli.

ex_en: Sabha is in the south.
note: Main city of the Fezzan region.

ex_en: Zawiya is close to Tripoli.
note: Coastal city west of Tripoli.

ex_en: The people of the neighborhood all know me.
note: pl. حوم 7wam. Very Libyan/Maghrebi; ولد حومة = a local guy from the area.

ex_en: The old city is very beautiful.
note: pl. مدن mudun. المدينة القديمة = Tripoli's old walled medina.

ex_en: My grandfather lives in a small village.
note: pl. قرى gura

ex_en: We live in a new apartment building.
note: pl. عمارات 3marāt

ex_en: Go over the bridge.
note: From Turkish köprü. pl. كباري kbāri. جسر jisr is also used.

ex_en: Stop at the traffic light.
note: Lit. "signal".

ex_en: Turn right at the roundabout.
note: Roundabouts are key landmarks when giving directions in Libyan cities.

ex_en: We stroll along the corniche at night.
note: From French corniche.

ex_en: You have to go to the municipality to get the document.
I have to go to the embassy to get a visa.
note: pl. سفارات

ex_en: I'll fill up with petrol at the station.
note: On its own it usually means a petrol station.

ex_ar: الحوش في الزنقة اللي ورا الجامع.
ex_en: The house is in the alley behind the mosque.
note: pl. زنقات zangāt

ex_en: Let's go downtown to shop.
note: Libyans often say just البلاد il-blād for "town center".

ex_en: The kids are playing in the park.
note: pl. حدائق 7adāyig

ex_ar: امشي على الرصيف مش في الطريق.
ex_en: Walk on the sidewalk, not in the road.
note: pl. أرصفة

ex_en: This building has ten floors.
note: pl. مباني mabāni

ex_en: I go to the club every day.
note: pl. نوادي nawādi. Tripoli clubs Al-Ahly and Al-Ittihad are football rivals.

ex_en: The cemetery is behind the mosque.
note: pl. مقابر magābir

ex_en: The airport is near Souq al-Juma.
note: Large district of eastern Tripoli; Mitiga airport is there.

ex_en: The Green Mountain is cold in winter.
note: Forested highland region in eastern Libya, around al-Bayda.

ex_en: My car is at the mechanic's.
note: From Italian macchina. pl. مكاين mkāyin. Very common Libyan word for car.

ex_en: I bought a new car.
note: pl. سيارات. More formal than مكينة makīna but widely used.

ex_en: In the old days people rode in horse carriages.
note: From Italian carrozza.

ex_en: Take a taxi to the airport.
The bus stops in front of the school.
note: From English. Formal: حافلة 7āfla.

ex_en: The plane takes off at nine o'clock.
note: pl. طيارات

ex_en: I'll drive you to the airport.
note: Tripoli's main airport is Mitiga (معيتيقة).

ex_en: Don't forget your passport!
note: Short for جواز سفر jawāz safar.

ex_en: I booked a ticket to Tunis.
note: pl. تذاكر tadhākir

ex_ar: نزلنا في فندق قريب من البحر.
ex_tr: nzilna fi fundug grīb min il-ba7ar.
ex_en: We stayed at a hotel near the sea.
note: pl. فنادق fanādig

ex_en: How was the trip?
note: pl. سفرات safrāt

ex_en: I love travelling a lot.
The flight was delayed two hours.
note: pl. رحلات. Also used for school or family outings.

ex_en: The suitcase is very heavy.
note: pl. شنط shunaT

ex_en: Turn to the right.
The bank is on the left.
Show me the map on the phone.
note: pl. خرائط kharāyiT

ex_en: The visa takes a month.
note: Formal: تأشيرة ta'shīra.

ex_en: The ship arrived at the port.
We travelled by ship to Malta.
note: From Italian vapore "steam(er)". pl. بوابير bwābīr

ex_en: The fishermen went out in the boat.
note: From Italian feluca. pl. فلايك flāyik

ex_en: My brother rides a motorbike.
note: From Italian moto.

ex_en: The little one wants a bicycle.
note: From Italian bicicletta via Maghrebi usage.

ex_en: Petrol is cheap in Libya.
note: From Italian benzina.

ex_en: I got my driving license last month.
note: pl. رخص rukhaS

ex_en: The tire is flat.
note: pl. عجلات. مفشوشة = deflated.

ex_en: Slowly, there's a speed bump.
We were stuck in traffic for an hour.
The driver took us home.
note: pl. سواقة sawwāga

ex_en: The passengers are waiting at the airport.
note: Also adj "travelling, away": هو مسافر = he's away.

ex_en: I have a reservation at the hotel.
They searched the suitcase at customs.
note: From Turkish gümrük.

ex_en: The border with Tunisia is crowded.
note: Ras Ajdir (راس جدير) is the main crossing to Tunisia.

ex_en: Benghazi is in the east.
Tripoli is in the west.
The sea is to the north.
The desert is in the south.
What is your address?
note: pl. عناوين 3anāwīn

ex_en: We're going to the sea on Friday.
note: pl. بحور b7ūr. Libyans say "the sea" for going to the beach.

ex_en: The beach is full of people in summer.
note: pl. شطوط shTūT

ex_en: The Libyan desert is huge.
The sand is hot at midday.
note: القايلة il-gāyla = the hot midday hours.

ex_en: We went up to the mountain in spring.
note: pl. جبال jbāl. الجبل often means the Nafusa Mountains (جبل نفوسة) in the west.

ex_en: Sit under the tree in the shade.
note: pl. شجر shjar (collective)

ex_en: The sun is scorching today.
The moon is full tonight.
note: Libyan/Maghrebi feminine form; قمر gamar also heard.

ex_en: The sky is full of stars.
note: pl. نجوم njūm

ex_en: The sky is clear today.
Rain is scarce in Libya.
note: See also شتا shta, the everyday Libyan word for rain.

ex_en: It's pouring rain outside!
note: Maghrebi double meaning: both "winter" and "rain".

ex_en: The wind is strong today.
note: pl. رياح

ex_en: The weather is nice today.
The heat is unbearable in August.
note: Also means "fever" colloquially.

ex_en: The cold at night is biting.
note: Also "a cold" (illness).

ex_en: The ghibli came and everything is dusty.
note: Hot, dry, dusty southerly wind; lit. "from the qibla/south". English "ghibli" comes from this.

en: dust storm; dust in the air
ex_en: Close the window, there's dust blowing.

ex_ar: في الصيف نمشوا للبحر كل يوم.
ex_en: In summer we go to the sea every day.
Autumn in Libya is short.
Spring is the nicest season.
What's your favorite season?
